Family Health

Nipple pain: causes, treatment and feeding support

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Nipple pain can come from something as simple as clothing rubbing the skin, but persistent pain deserves attention. The timing, appearance of the skin and any changes elsewhere in the breast help guide assessment. Treatment works best when it addresses the cause rather than repeatedly covering the discomfort with a cream or painkiller.

Start with the pattern of the pain

Notice whether one nipple or both are affected, when the pain began and whether it follows a menstrual pattern. Does it happen during a feed, after pumping, when clothing rubs, or even without touch? Cracks, a rash, discharge, a lump or a change in nipple shape are useful details to report.

A poorly fitting bra or a tight, rough shirt can repeatedly irritate sensitive skin. Try a comfortable fit and soft fabric that reduce rubbing without squeezing the breast. Breast size can change over time, especially during pregnancy and feeding, so a size that once fitted may no longer be suitable.

If there is no clear explanation, the pain is not improving, or a new breast change appears, arrange an examination. Most breast pain is not caused by cancer, but that reassurance should not be used to dismiss a persistent symptom.

Hormonal changes around periods and pregnancy

Breasts can feel swollen, heavy or tender before a period as hormone levels change. Cyclical pain often affects both sides and eases as the period ends. Keeping a brief symptom record can help distinguish this pattern from pain that remains in one place throughout the month.

Pregnancy can also make the breasts larger and more sensitive. Small bumps around the areola may become more noticeable; these Montgomery glands are a normal part of breast anatomy. Tender breasts, a missed period, nausea or vomiting, tiredness and needing to urinate more often can accompany early pregnancy, but symptoms alone do not confirm it.

If pregnancy is possible, take a pregnancy test and ask for advice if the result or symptoms are unclear. A blood test is not automatically needed for everyone. Breast tenderness may change as pregnancy progresses; ongoing growth does not mean all pain is harmless or that it must disappear on a fixed schedule.

Look for skin irritation or eczema

Dry, itchy, flaky or crusted skin around the nipple or areola can be caused by dermatitis. Some people also develop weeping areas or small blisters. Irritant reactions can follow soaps, detergents, fragrances or clothing; an allergic reaction can occur to an ingredient in a cream or other product.

Avoid an obvious trigger and seek advice about a simple moisturizer or treatment. A clinician may prescribe a suitable topical steroid for eczema, but strength, duration and application matter on this delicate skin. During breastfeeding, ask exactly how to use the product and whether it must be removed before the next feed.

Do not repeatedly treat a persistent rash on one nipple as eczema without a diagnosis. Several conditions look similar, including the uncommon breast condition called Paget disease. A rash that does not settle, especially with a new nipple change or discharge, needs assessment.

Breastfeeding pain needs practical help

Nipple discomfort is common at the beginning of breastfeeding, but pain at every feed, cracking or bleeding is a reason to get help promptly. The baby’s position and attachment are often important. A shallow latch may compress the nipple rather than allowing comfortable feeding.

Ask a midwife, lactation consultant or other skilled feeding professional to watch an entire feed. They can assess attachment, your comfort and how the baby is transferring milk. Trying another supported position may help, but repeatedly changing positions is not a substitute for finding the cause.

A breast pump can also injure the nipple if the flange does not fit comfortably, suction is too strong or the session is uncomfortable. Follow the pump instructions, start at a low setting and check that the nipple sits comfortably in the opening. Pumping should not cause ongoing pain, skin damage or bleeding; get help adjusting the equipment rather than increasing suction to push through.

Mastitis is inflammation, sometimes with infection

Mastitis can cause a hot, swollen, painful area of the breast, sometimes with redness, fever, chills or flu-like symptoms. Redness may be less obvious on darker skin. It is not always a bacterial infection, and antibiotics are not required for every episode.

Seek prompt medical advice for fever with a painful breast, spreading redness or feeling unwell. A clinician can decide whether antibiotics or further assessment are needed. A persistent or worsening lump may need an ultrasound to look for an abscess, which is a collection of pus that may require drainage.

Continue usual responsive feeding if you can and obtain a plan if pain prevents it. Avoid aggressive massage or extra pumping intended to empty the breast. These can worsen inflammation. A cool compress and suitable pain relief may help; prolonged heat is not a universal treatment. If symptoms are not improving within 12–24 hours, or worsen sooner, seek further advice.

Do not assume every burning pain is thrush

Thrush is a yeast infection that can affect a baby’s mouth or the nipple surface. Burning after feeds, itching or changes in the nipple’s skin can prompt assessment. White patches in a baby’s mouth that do not wipe away easily may also need checking.

These signs are not enough to diagnose every case of breast or nipple pain as thrush. Attachment problems, eczema and blood-vessel spasm can produce overlapping symptoms. Whether Candida explains deep breast pain is disputed in clinical guidance, so persistent pain should be evaluated rather than treated repeatedly with antifungal medicine on assumption.

If a clinician diagnoses thrush, they may recommend an antifungal treatment and assess whether the baby also needs treatment. Follow instructions for the specific product, including its use around feeds. Do not use an adult preparation in the baby’s mouth or keep adding treatments if symptoms continue without reassessment.

Choose comfort measures for the actual cause

Reducing friction and finding a supportive, comfortable bra can help. Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, or ibuprofen may be suitable for some people, but check with a pharmacist or clinician if you are pregnant, have another health condition or take other medicines. These are different medicines; check active ingredients rather than relying on brand names.

Warmth may soothe certain types of discomfort, but an inflamed, swollen breast often benefits more from cooling. Ask for advice when pain follows cold exposure or comes with nipple color changes, since a blood-vessel spasm may need a different approach. Avoid very hot compresses and stop anything that irritates the skin.

Lanolin is sometimes used for sore nipples, but it is not a guaranteed way to prevent cracks and cannot correct attachment or pump trauma. It can also cause contact allergy in some people. Ask which product, if any, fits your situation and stop using a product that worsens redness, itching or soreness. Skin treatments should not delay help for a persistent breast change.

Reducing recurrent pain without over-treating

For symptoms linked to periods, a diary, a comfortable bra and an appropriate pain-relief plan are useful starting points. There is not good evidence that caffeine causes breast cysts. Some people report less discomfort when they reduce caffeine, but it should not be presented as a proven prevention strategy.

Similarly, cutting salt or exercising specifically to flush out fluid is not an established cure for nipple pain. Regular activity and a balanced diet can support general wellbeing without replacing an assessment. If cyclical pain is troublesome, discuss medicines or hormonal contraception with a clinician: a hormonal method may help some people but can itself cause breast tenderness.

During breastfeeding, respond to the baby’s feeding needs and ask for help with uncomfortable fullness. Do not add frequent pumping solely to prevent soreness or always start on the painful breast as a rule. A feeding plan should balance comfort, the baby’s intake and milk production. Addressing attachment and pump fit is more useful than relying on repeated creams.

Changes that should be examined

Arrange prompt assessment for a new lump, a nipple that has newly turned inward, unexpected discharge (particularly blood-stained discharge) or a persistent rash, scaling or redness. A change in one breast’s size or shape, or skin dimpling, also needs review.

Pain alone is unlikely to be a sign of breast cancer. Still, these associated changes should be checked even when they are not painful, and breastfeeding or pregnancy does not make a new lump something to ignore. A feverish, hot or rapidly swelling breast needs urgent advice because infection or an abscess may need treatment.

If you become severely unwell, faint, confused or short of breath, seek emergency help. Otherwise, contact a clinician when pain persists despite simple adjustments or interferes with feeding or daily life. It is reasonable to ask for reassessment when an initial treatment has not helped.

How clinicians investigate the cause

The consultation usually begins with questions about symptoms, periods, pregnancy possibility, feeding, medicines and family history, followed by an examination of the breasts and nipples. A skin problem or feeding difficulty may be assessed differently from a new lump.

A diagnostic mammogram uses X-rays to examine an area of concern; this is different in purpose from a routine screening appointment. Ultrasound uses sound waves and can help distinguish a fluid-filled cyst from a solid area. A solid finding is not automatically cancer, and imaging alone does not settle every diagnosis.

If tissue needs to be checked, a biopsy removes cells or a small sample for examination in a laboratory. The choice of tests depends on the examination, age, pregnancy or lactation and other factors. Not everyone with nipple pain needs every test.

Treatment and outlook depend on the diagnosis

Friction may improve after changing clothing, and a cyclical pattern may settle as the menstrual phase changes. Eczema may need ongoing trigger avoidance and treatment when it flares. Feeding-related injury usually requires correction of the mechanical cause; a diagnosed infection needs the appropriate treatment and follow-up.

If breast cancer is diagnosed, the care team plans treatment according to its type, stage and biological features. Options can include surgery to remove a tumor or the breast, radiation, chemotherapy, hormone-blocking treatment for hormone-sensitive disease, and targeted medicines. People do not necessarily need every treatment.

The outlook cannot be predicted from nipple pain itself. Ask what improvement to expect, how long to try the agreed plan and which changes should trigger an earlier review. You deserve support with the discomfort while the cause is being investigated.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pain alone is usually not a cancer symptom, but persistent nipple or breast changes still require examination.

Feeding assessment and pump fit are central when pain is linked to milk feeding; mastitis care should distinguish inflammation from bacterial infection.

Evidence and clinical guidance differ on Candida as a cause of deep breast pain. Symptoms should not automatically lead to repeated antifungal treatment.

How BeMama can help

Record when the pain happens and bring the bra, pump details or feeding questions that may help explain it. One observed feed or equipment check can make the next step more specific.

When to seek help

Seek prompt care for a hot swollen breast, fever, a new lump, blood-stained discharge, new nipple inversion or a persistent one-sided nipple rash. Severe systemic illness needs emergency assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Look at timing, skin changes and feeding or clothing triggers.
  • Persistent pain, a lump or a new nipple change deserves assessment.
  • Painful feeding is a reason to get skilled help, not something to endure indefinitely.
  • Mastitis does not always require antibiotics; burning pain does not automatically mean thrush.
  • Match creams, medicines and comfort measures to the cause.

Frequently asked questions

What treatment helps nipple pain?

It depends on the cause. A better clothing fit, feeding or pump adjustment, eczema treatment or infection treatment may be needed. Pain relief can help symptoms but should not replace assessment of persistent pain.

How is the cause diagnosed?

A clinician asks about the pattern and examines the breast and nipple. They may observe feeding, assess the skin, arrange a pregnancy test or request imaging or biopsy when indicated.

Can I prevent soreness before a period?

A symptom diary, a comfortable bra and an agreed pain-relief plan may help. Caffeine avoidance, salt restriction and exercising to remove fluid are not proven universal solutions. Ask about troublesome recurrent symptoms.

How can I reduce nipple pain while breastfeeding?

Get attachment and positioning checked and make sure a pump fits comfortably. Feed responsively and avoid unnecessary extra pumping. Cracks, bleeding or pain at every feed need early help.

Does nipple pain mean breast cancer?

Usually not when pain is the only symptom. A new lump, unexpected discharge, inversion, skin dimpling or a persistent nipple rash still needs examination.

Should I put lanolin on every sore nipple?

No single cream suits every cause. Lanolin cannot fix feeding trauma and can irritate some people. Ask about suitable skin care and stop a product that worsens symptoms.

Does mastitis always need antibiotics?

No. Mastitis includes inflammation that may settle with appropriate supportive care and bacterial infection that may need antibiotics. A clinician should assess worsening or persistent symptoms.

Is burning after feeding always thrush?

No. Several conditions can cause similar pain. Ask for an examination and feeding assessment before repeated antifungal treatment, especially when pain is deep in the breast or treatment has not helped.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
